title: The Tiny Fossil That Fooled Scientists for Nearly 30 Years
summary:
For almost 30 years, scientists thought a tiny fossil from Scotland was an early reptile. They named it Westlothiana lizziae and nicknamed it Lizzie because it looked like a lizard.

Lizzie's fossil is 345 million years old and was found in 1984. It is a nearly whole skeleton, squashed flat between two slabs of rock. Studied in 1990, it showed only its outside. Legs with fingers and toes, some with claw-like tips, made it look ready for land. So scientists called Lizzie the earliest known amniote, a group that includes reptiles, birds, and mammals.

But X-ray scans told a different story. Scientists from the American Museum of Natural History and the University of Oxford used X-rays to look inside it in Grenoble, France. Lizzie had a simple skull, gills with bone inside, and a fish-like mouth full of thousands of tiny teeth. So it lived in water, not on land.

Shared in Nature, the find shows claws and five fingers and toes may have first appeared in water animals. Footprints with clawed toes do not prove reptiles walked there.
why_it_matters: It shows that asking questions and looking closer can change what everyone thinks is true, just like checking your own work can catch a mistake.

background_read: A fossil is the remains of a living thing from long ago, kept in rock, and scientists study fossils to learn how animals lived.
Lizzie looked like an early land animal from the outside, but X-ray scans let scientists see inside the fossil without breaking it.
The scans showed Lizzie lived in water, so the find changed what scientists thought about early animals with claws and five fingers and toes.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists from the American Museum of Natural History and the University of Oxford, and a tiny fossil they nicknamed Lizzie.
WHAT: X-ray scans showed Lizzie was a water animal, not the earliest known land animal.
WHERE: In Scotland, where the fossil was found, and in Grenoble, France, where the scans were done.
WHY: Because the find changes what scientists thought about when claws and five fingers and toes first appeared.

perspectives.description: They thought Lizzie was the earliest known amniote because its legs and claw-like toes looked ready for land.
They found gills and a fish-like mouth inside, so they say Lizzie lived in water, not on land.
